01.note: Mar, son of Ravina, was once walking through a valley of willows and grew thirsty; a miracle happened and a spring of water appeared for him, and he drank. Another time, in the marketplace of Mehoza, a wild camel attacked him; a wall cracked open, he went inside it and was rescued. From then on, whenever he came to the willows or to the Mehoza marketplace, he recited a blessing thanking God who performed a miracle for him there, naming both miracles.
01.why: The Gemara has asked whether a blessing is said only for a miracle done for the whole people. Mar's practice shows an individual blesses for his own miracle, and the Sages conclude: everyone blesses for a public miracle, only the person himself for a private one.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Sage who was saved by two miracles, a spring in the willows and escape from a wild camel, and blessed God at both places.

terms.term: Blessed…Who performed a miracle for me
terms.meaning: A short blessing said when returning to a place where one was miraculously saved. The dots stand for the standard opening, Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe.

02.note: Rav Ketina was walking along a road and, as he reached the door of a necromancer, the ground rumbled in an earthquake. He wondered aloud whether the necromancer knew what the earthquake was. The necromancer called out, Ketina, Ketina, why would I not know? When God remembers His children suffering among the nations, He sheds two tears into the great sea, and the sound is heard from one end of the world to the other. Rav Ketina declared the necromancer a liar, since two tears should make two quakes; the Gemara remarks that there are in fact two, and Rav Ketina refused to admit it so that people would not be led astray after the necromancer.
02.why: The mishna requires a blessing over zeva'ot, and Rav Ketina defines the word as an earthquake. The story leads into a list of the Sages' explanations of what causes earthquakes, and then thunder and wind, all phenomena over which that blessing is said.

people.name: Rav Ketina
people.about: A Sage who defined zeva'ot as an earthquake and who met the necromancer on the road.

terms.meaning: Someone who claims to consult the dead. The Torah forbids this practice, which is why Rav Ketina would not let people credit what he said.
A word in the mishna for a natural event over which one says the blessing praising God whose strength and power fill the world. Rav Ketina explains it as earthquakes.

03.note: Rabbi Akiva came to a town and asked for lodging, but no one would give him any. He said, Everything God does is for the best, and slept in a field with his rooster, his donkey and a candle. The wind blew out the candle, a cat ate the rooster and a lion ate the donkey, and again he said, Everything God does is for the best. That night an army came and took the town captive; as the translation explains, he alone was saved, with no light, crowing rooster or donkey to give him away. He said, Didn't I tell you? Everything God does is for the best.
03.why: The Gemara has cited a teaching in Rabbi Akiva's name that a person should always train himself to say that everything God does is for the best. This story is told as the example of Rabbi Akiva living by his own teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who was refused lodging, lost his animals and light in the night, and was spared when the town was captured.

04.note: Shammai and Hillel disagreed over whether grapes harvested for the winepress can become ritually impure. Hillel challenged Shammai: why harvest grapes in purity but not olives? Shammai answered that if Hillel provoked him, he would decree impurity on olives too. A sword was stuck into the study hall and it was announced that anyone could enter but no one could leave. That day Hillel sat bowed before Shammai like a student, and the Gemara says it was as hard for Israel as the day the Golden Calf was made. Shammai and Hillel issued the decree and the people did not accept it; their students later issued it and the people accepted it.
04.why: The Gemara is counting the eighteen decrees the Sages passed on one famous day and needs to complete the tally. The decree about harvested grapes is given as another of the eighteen; afterward the Gemara asks what the reason for that decree was.

people.name: Hillel
people.about: Head of the Sages in his day; here he argued against the decree and was forced to sit before Shammai like a student.

people.name: Shammai
people.about: Hillel's colleague and opponent, who held that harvested grapes become susceptible to impurity and threatened to extend the decree to olives.

terms.meaning: In Jewish purity law, food can only become ritually impure after it has been moistened by certain liquids. The question is whether juice seeping from grapes during harvest counts.
Using ritually pure vessels and hands, so that the produce stays pure.
The idol the Israelites made in the desert (Exodus 32), remembered as one of the worst days in the nation's history.

05.note: Rabbi Zeira wanted to move from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, but his teacher Rav Yehuda held that leaving Babylonia for the Land of Israel violates a commandment, so Rabbi Zeira was avoiding him. Before leaving he decided to go and hear one more teaching from him. He found Rav Yehuda in the bathhouse telling his servant: bring me natron, bring me a comb, open your mouths and let out air, and drink from the bathhouse water. Rabbi Zeira said that had he come only to hear this, it would have been enough.
05.why: The Gemara has been discussing proper conduct while bathing. After the story it draws lessons from each of Rav Yehuda's instructions, such as that ordinary matters may be spoken in Hebrew in a bathhouse and why drinking hot water while bathing is healthy.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Rav Yehuda's student, who wanted to emigrate to the Land of Israel against his teacher's view.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rabbi Zeira's teacher, who held it was forbidden to leave Babylonia for the Land of Israel.

terms.meaning: The Land of Israel.
A natural mineral salt used as soap for washing.

06.note: After bloodletting, Shmuel, Rav Yehuda and Rabba each needed a fire to keep warm. For Shmuel they broke up a teak armchair, for Rav Yehuda an ebony table, and for Rabba a bench, to use as fuel. Abaye asked Rabba whether breaking the bench did not violate the commandment 'Do not destroy'. Rabba answered that not destroying his own body mattered more to him.
06.why: Shmuel has ruled that a fire may be made on Shabbat for someone who let blood and caught cold, even in midsummer. These cases show how seriously the Sages took the danger of cold after bloodletting, even burning valuable furniture.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage for whom a teak armchair was broken up for a fire after bloodletting.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage for whom an ebony table was broken up for a fire.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage for whom a bench was broken up; he defended it to Abaye.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, who asked whether breaking the bench was wasteful destruction.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment, common in ancient times. The person was considered weakened and at risk afterward.
A Torah prohibition (Deuteronomy 20:19) against needlessly destroying useful or valuable things.

07.note: Ablat, a gentile scholar, found Shmuel lying in the sun. He asked him, Wise man of the Jews, can something harmful become good? Shmuel answered that on a day of bloodletting the sun is good for a person. The Gemara comments that this was not really so: there is one day in the year when the sun is beneficial, the day of the summer solstice, and Shmuel did not want to reveal that remedy to Ablat.
07.why: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak has just advised that someone who let blood and has nothing to eat should lie in the sun. The story shows Shmuel doing so, and the Gemara adds that his stated reason was a cover.

people.name: Ablat
people.about: A gentile scholar who found Shmuel lying in the sun and questioned him.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage, called by Ablat the wise man of the Jews.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood from the body as a medical treatment; the person was considered weakened afterward and needed warmth and food.
The summer solstice, the longest day of the year, which falls around the Hebrew month of Tammuz.

08.note: When Rabbi Hanina's daughter died, he did not cry over her. His wife asked him whether he had merely let a chicken out of the house. He answered that if he cried he would suffer twice: from the loss and from blindness. The Gemara explains that he followed a teaching that some tears are bad for the eyes, among them tears of crying out of grief.
08.why: The discussion has just cited Shmuel's statement that after age forty, tears permanently weaken the eyesight. Rabbi Hanina's refusal to weep for his daughter puts that belief into practice.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who did not weep when his daughter died, for fear of losing his sight.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who reported the teaching about good and bad tears.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei ben Ketzarta
people.about: The Sage in whose name Rabbi Yohanan taught that there are six kinds of tears.

09.note: A man from the valley of Beit Hortan stuck four poles into the four corners of his field and stretched a vine across the top of them. According to the translation, he meant this to count as a wall around the field, so that he could plant near a vineyard without breaking the rule against mixing crops. The case came before the Sages, and they permitted it for the purpose of diverse kinds.
09.why: The Gemara wants to show that Rabbi Yohanan agrees with Rav that a doorway-shaped opening does not count as a wall if it is very wide. It cites this case, on which Reish Lakish says the field also counts as enclosed for Shabbat and Rabbi Yohanan says it does not.

terms.meaning: The Torah's ban on planting certain mixed crops together, including grain or vegetables too close to a vineyard. A proper wall between them removes the problem.
Two upright posts with a crosspiece on top. In Jewish law it can count as a wall with a doorway in it, closing off an area.

10.note: Rav Nahman taught publicly, in the name of Shmuel, that one or two travelers may enclose an area of two beit se'a, and three, who count as a caravan, may enclose six. He was asked whether he had abandoned the majority view of the Rabbis to follow the lone opinion of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Nahman then had a speaker stand beside him and announced: What I told you was my error. He restated the rule so that a caravan of three is given as much space as it needs.
10.why: The Mishna and a baraita record a dispute over how much space travelers may enclose with makeshift partitions for carrying on Shabbat. After the story the Gemara asks whether Rav Nahman's corrected ruling mixes the two opposing views, and why that is allowed.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who taught a ruling in public and then publicly retracted it as a mistake.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Nahman's teacher, called here Rabbeinu Shmuel, in whose name he taught.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: An earlier Sage whose minority view Rav Nahman was accused of following.

terms.meaning: A unit of area, roughly the field needed to sow a se'a of grain; two beit se'a is the area of the Tabernacle courtyard, about 5,000 square cubits.
A group of three or more travelers, who are given a larger area in which they may carry on Shabbat.
A person who stood beside a Sage teaching in public and announced his words loudly to the audience.

11.note: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata brought a basket of fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya on the eve of Shabbat. As he was leaving, Rav Natan let him go down one step and then told him, Stay here tonight. The next morning Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata got up early and went home.
11.why: Ulla has ruled that a traveler who set out and was persuaded to turn back still counts as having set out, which affects how far he may walk on Shabbat. The Gemara then asks which Sages' views Rav Natan was following when he let his guest start out before inviting him to stay.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata
people.about: A Sage who brought a basket of fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya before Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Oshaya
people.about: The host, who let his guest set out and then asked him to stay the night.

terms.meaning: On Shabbat a person may walk only a set distance (2,000 cubits) beyond his place of residence. Someone who sets out toward a point at the edge of that limit can count it as his residence and go 2,000 more.

12.note: One of Rabbi Eliezer's students issued a legal ruling in his presence. Rabbi Eliezer told his wife, Imma Shalom, that he would be surprised if this student lived out the year, and he did not live out the year. She asked him whether he was a prophet. He said he was not a prophet or the son of a prophet, but he had received a tradition: anyone who issues a ruling in his teacher's presence is liable to death.
12.why: Rava has ruled that a student who rules in his teacher's presence is liable to death but one who rules elsewhere is not. The Gemara tests this against the story, since a later report says the student was three parasangs away, and concludes the ruling was given in the teacher's presence.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage whose student ruled in his presence; he predicted the student would die within the year.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's wife, who asked him if he was a prophet.

terms.meaning: Here, deserving death at the hands of Heaven, not a punishment carried out by a court.

13.note: On a Shabbat, the warm water prepared for a baby's circumcision spilled. Rava had water in his own courtyard, and he told people to move his belongings from his men's room to the inner women's room; he would sit there and give up his rights to his courtyard so the water could be brought over. Ravina challenged him with Shmuel's view that rights cannot be given up from one courtyard to another, and Rava said he followed Rabbi Yohanan. Ravina asked why, then, Rava did not stay put and have the neighbors give their rights back afterward, as Rav allowed. Rava said that on that point he followed Shmuel, and the two argued over whether Shmuel's two rulings rest on the same reason. The text does not say what was finally done.
13.why: The Gemara is telling several incidents of circumcision water spilled on Shabbat. This one turns on the dispute between Rav and Shmuel about giving up and returning rights in a courtyard, which the Gemara then examines directly.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who offered to give up the rights to his courtyard so the baby's water could be carried.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who challenged Rava's plan with Shmuel's rulings.

terms.meaning: When neighbors sharing a courtyard did not set up an eiruv, one may give up his share of the courtyard for Shabbat, so the others may carry there.
An arrangement, made before Shabbat, that turns several homes and a shared courtyard into one domain so that carrying between them is allowed.
The outer room of a house, opening onto the courtyard; the women's chamber was an inner room that did not.

14.note: A Sadducee lived in the same alleyway in Jerusalem as Rabban Gamliel and gave up his rights to the alleyway before Shabbat. Rabban Gamliel told his sons to hurry and take out and bring in whatever they needed before that loathsome man took out his own things and made the alleyway forbidden to them. In another version, given by Rabbi Yehuda, he told them to hurry and do what they needed in the alleyway before nightfall.
14.why: The mishna mentions a Sadducee where the discussion was about gentiles, and the Gemara explains that a clause is missing: Rabban Gamliel holds that a Sadducee is not like a gentile in these laws. The incident shows him treating the Sadducee's renunciation as valid.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A Sage, who in one version tells of his father's ruling and in another tells his own sons what to do.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage whose version of Rabban Gamliel's words is given first.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who reports Rabban Gamliel's words differently.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group of the Second Temple period that rejected the Sages' oral tradition.
A member of a group similar to the Sadducees that also rejected the Sages' tradition.
Gave up his share in a shared space for Shabbat, so that the other residents may carry there without an eiruv.

15.note: Rabbi Oshaya's daughter-in-law went to the bathhouse before Shabbat, and it grew dark before she could get back. Her mother-in-law made an eiruv for her so she could return home. The case came before Rabbi Hiyya, who ruled it invalid and forbade her return. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, protested: Babylonian, are you so strict about eiruvin? My father said, wherever you can be lenient with an eiruv, be lenient.
15.why: Rav holds that a Shabbat-boundary eiruv works only if the food is formally transferred to the person it serves; the Gemara says this is an older dispute and cites the case. Afterward it asks whether Rabbi Hiyya forbade it for lack of transfer or because she did not know of it.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: The Sage who ruled the mother-in-law's eiruv invalid.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who objected to Rabbi Hiyya's strictness, quoting his father.

people.name: Rabbi Oshaya
people.about: The father-in-law of the woman stranded at the bathhouse.

terms.meaning: An eiruv of food placed before Shabbat at a spot, letting a person count that spot as home and so walk farther than the usual Shabbat limit.
Rabbi Hiyya had come from Babylonia to the Land of Israel; the address points to his origin.

16.note: The son of Bonyas came before Rabbi, who told his attendants to make room for a man worth a hundred maneh. Another man came, and Rabbi said to make room for a man worth two hundred maneh. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, told him that the first visitor's father owned a thousand ships at sea and a thousand towns on land. Rabbi replied: when you see his father, tell him not to send his son to me in such clothes.
16.why: The mishna's example of a landlord's right of usage is the courtyard of the wealthy Bonyas, so the Gemara adds this story about his wealth. Afterward it explains that Rabbi, like Rabbi Akiva, made a point of honoring the rich.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, head of the Sages, who greeted visitors according to their apparent wealth.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who told Rabbi how rich the first visitor's father really was.

people.name: son of Bonyas
people.about: The son of an extremely wealthy man, who came to Rabbi in modest clothes.

terms.meaning: A large unit of money, equal to one hundred zuz. A man worth a hundred maneh was very wealthy.

17.note: Rav Dimi reported an incident in Tzippori: the people forgot to bring a Torah scroll to the synagogue before Shabbat. The next day, Shabbat, they spread a sheet over the pillars along the way, brought the scroll through the enclosed path and read from it. The Gemara objects that putting up even a temporary tent is forbidden on Shabbat, and corrects the account: they found sheets already spread over the pillars, and used them to bring the scroll and read.
17.why: The Gemara has argued that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei need not agree about walls that hang down without reaching the ground. The Tzippori incident seemed to rely on such walls, so it says it was done on the authority of Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported what happened in Tzippori.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage on whose authority the Tzippori incident was carried out.

terms.meaning: Any makeshift roof or covering. Putting one up counts as building and is forbidden on Shabbat.
From the outset; describing what one may do in the first place, as opposed to what is accepted after the fact.

18.note: Rabbi recalled that when he and others studied Torah with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa, they would carry oil and a towel from roof to roof, roof to courtyard, courtyard to courtyard, courtyard to enclosure and enclosure to enclosure, until they reached the spring where they bathed. Rabbi Yehuda recalled a time of danger when they carried a Torah scroll from courtyard to roof, roof to courtyard and courtyard to enclosure in order to read from it. The Sages answered him that a time of danger is no proof.
18.why: The Gemara is weighing how Rav and Rav Yehuda each read the opinions on carrying between roofs, courtyards and enclosures. These memories are a baraita supporting Rav Yehuda's reading that for Rabbi Shimon all of them count as one domain.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who recalled studying with Rabbi Shimon in Tekoa.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi's teacher in Tekoa, in whose presence the students carried between roofs, courtyards and enclosures.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who recalled carrying a Torah scroll in a time of danger.

terms.meaning: A fenced area, such as a yard for storage, that is not attached to a house.
A period of persecution when the authorities banned Jewish religious practice.

19.note: A man left a saddlebag full of leavened bread in the care of Yohanan Hakuka'a. Mice gnawed a hole in it, and the bread began spilling out. On the day before Passover, Yohanan came to Rabbi to ask what to do. In the first, second, third and fourth hours Rabbi told him to wait; in the fifth hour he told him, Go and sell it in the market.
19.why: The Gemara claims Rabbi agrees with the ruling that follows Rabbi Yehuda on how late on Passover eve leaven is allowed. Afterward it debates whether Rabbi meant selling to gentiles or to a Jew, and why Yohanan could not just keep the bread himself.

people.name: Yohanan Hakuka'a
people.about: The man entrusted with the saddlebag of leavened bread, who asked Rabbi what to do.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who told him to wait hour by hour and then to sell it.

terms.meaning: Bread or food that has risen, called hametz. It may not be eaten or owned on Passover and must be gone by midday on the day before.
Hours are counted from morning, so the fifth hour is late morning, shortly before leaven becomes fully forbidden at the sixth hour.

20.note: Rav Ya'akov bar Abba visited Rava's house and saw him say the blessing over wine on the first cup, and then say it again over the cup of Grace after Meals. He asked why, since Rava had already blessed once. Rava said that was their practice at the Exilarch's house. Rav Ya'akov answered that there they never knew whether another cup would come, but here the cup was right in front of them. Rava said he followed Rav's students: Rav Beruna and Rav Hananel were eating, served by Rav Yeiva the Elder. They asked for a cup to say Grace, then changed their minds and asked for one to drink. Rav Yeiva told them that Rav had said that once they asked for the Grace cup, they could not drink without a new blessing, since they had turned their minds away from drinking.
20.why: The Gemara has been discussing the order of blessings at a meal. After the story it brings three Sages with three different practices about wine blessings, and Rav Ashi rules against Rav's students.

people.name: Rav Ya'akov bar Abba
people.about: A visitor at Rava's house who questioned his second blessing over wine.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The host, who said the wine blessing twice and defended the practice.

people.name: Rav Beruna
people.about: One of Rav's students in the story Rava tells.

people.name: Rav Hananel
people.about: One of Rav's students, eating with Rav Beruna.

people.name: Rav Yeiva the Elder
people.about: The Sage who served the two students and told them Rav's ruling.

terms.term: Who creates the fruit of the vine
terms.meaning: The closing words of the blessing said before drinking wine.
The blessings said after eating a meal with bread, often recited over a cup of wine.
The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia; Sages often dined at his house.
